takeaways: A communication system is source, transmitter, channel, receiver and destination; the channel attenuates the signal and adds noise, r(t) = s(t) + n(t).

Modulation moves the message spectrum to a carrier for antenna size, frequency assignment, multiplexing, interference rejection and propagation; it creates no information and does not by itself raise the input SNR.

The Fourier transform turns filtering into multiplication and modulation into shifting: x(t)cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) has two half-height copies at ±f<sub>c</sub>, and its band-pass bandwidth is twice the baseband one.
A band-pass signal is fully described by its complex envelope x̃ = x<sub>I</sub> + j x<sub>Q</sub>, found with the Hilbert transform (cos → sin) and a shift by f<sub>c</sub>.
Probability is an area under the PDF; the Gaussian tail Q(z) with z = (x − μ)/σ gives threshold and error probabilities, and Bayes' rule turns likelihoods into posteriors.
For a WSS process the autocorrelation and the PSD are a Fourier pair; R<sub>X</sub>(0) is the power, and a filter multiplies the PSD by |H(f)|².

White noise is a model with infinite power; in a bandwidth B it gives N<sub>0</sub>B, which for thermal noise is kTB, −174 dBm/Hz + 10 log<sub>10</sub>B. Use the equivalent noise bandwidth for real filters.
Noise figure and noise temperature measure what a stage adds; in a cascade the first stage dominates (Friis), so a low-noise amplifier goes first and loss before it is costly.

Show every conversion between dB and linear values, and keep units on every power and temperature.

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of a communication system and explain, with numbers, why modulation is needed.
outline: Information source with input transducer, transmitter, channel with added noise, receiver, destination with output transducer; signals m(t), s(t), r(t) = s(t) + n(t) and the estimate
Antenna size: λ = c/f and λ/4; 1 kHz needs 75 km, 100 MHz needs 0.75 m
Frequency assignment by the regulator; baseband signals cannot share free space
Multiplexing: carriers spaced by the signal bandwidth (FDM)
Noise and interference: the receiver filter keeps only f<sub>c</sub> ± B<sub>s</sub>/2; propagation suits the carrier
Modulation moves the spectrum; it creates no information and does not by itself raise the input SNR
answer: Block diagram (draw left to right): information source and input transducer → transmitter → channel → receiver → destination and output transducer, with a noise source n(t) feeding the channel. The source gives the message m(t); the transmitter filters, modulates and amplifies it into s(t); the channel attenuates s(t) and adds noise, so the receiver gets r(t) = s(t) + n(t); the receiver filters, amplifies and demodulates to give the estimate m̂(t).

State the idea: modulation varies a carrier cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) with m(t). It copies the message spectrum to ±f<sub>c</sub>; it adds no information. A message of bandwidth B becomes, for AM, a signal of bandwidth B<sub>s</sub> = 2B centred on f<sub>c</sub>.

answer.text: Reason 1, antenna size. An antenna radiates well when it is about a quarter wavelength long, λ/4 = c/(4f) with c = 3×10<sup>8</sup> m/s:

answer: So a 1 kHz tone would need a 75 km antenna, while on a 100 MHz carrier it needs 0.75 m: smaller by 75 km ÷ 0.75 m = 10<sup>5</sup>, the ratio of the frequencies.

Reason 2, frequency assignment. Every baseband audio signal occupies the same range, about 0 to 5 kHz. If all stations radiated at baseband they would overlap. Regulators give each service its own band, and modulation places the signal in it.

Reason 3, multiplexing (FDM). With AM, a 5 kHz message takes 2B = 10 kHz, so carriers 10 kHz apart do not overlap. One megahertz of spectrum then holds 1 MHz ÷ 10 kHz = 100 programmes, which one cable or one antenna can carry at once.

Reason 4, noise and interference. Modulation does not remove noise, but the receiver's band-pass filter passes only f<sub>c</sub> − B<sub>s</sub>/2 to f<sub>c</sub> + B<sub>s</sub>/2 (for a 1 MHz AM station with B = 5 kHz, 0.995 to 1.005 MHz) and rejects every signal outside it. Wideband schemes such as FM go further and trade bandwidth for a better output SNR.

Reason 5, propagation. The carrier frequency decides how the wave travels: medium-wave signals near 1 MHz follow the ground for long distances, while VHF and higher frequencies travel in near line of sight. The carrier is chosen to suit the range needed.

Close with the limit: modulation shifts the spectrum and makes antennas, frequency plans and multiplexing practical; the SNR at the receiver input is still set by signal power and noise power in the band. Check: the antenna ratio 10<sup>5</sup> equals 100 MHz ÷ 1 kHz, as λ ∝ 1/f requires.

bank.q: State the Fourier transform and its inverse, and explain the four properties that are used most in modulation analysis.
outline: X(f) = ∫x(t)e<sup>−j2πft</sup>dt and x(t) = ∫X(f)e<sup>j2πft</sup>df; units V/Hz
Linearity
Frequency shift and the modulation theorem: x(t)cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) ↔ ½X(f − f<sub>c</sub>) + ½X(f + f<sub>c</sub>)
Convolution theorem: filtering is multiplication by H(f)
Parseval's (Rayleigh's) energy theorem, with a numerical check on a pulse
answer: Definitions: X(f) = ∫ x(t) e<sup>−j2πft</sup> dt and x(t) = ∫ X(f) e<sup>j2πft</sup> df, both integrals over (−∞, ∞). If x(t) is in volts, X(f) is in V/Hz, a density in frequency. |X(f)| is the magnitude spectrum and ∠X(f) the phase spectrum.

Linearity: a x<sub>1</sub>(t) + b x<sub>2</sub>(t) ↔ a X<sub>1</sub>(f) + b X<sub>2</sub>(f), because the integral is linear. It lets a signal made of several tones or pulses be transformed term by term; every AM and DSB-SC spectrum is built this way.

answer.text: Frequency shift and the modulation theorem. Substituting into the definition:
answer.pre:
∫ x(t) e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup> e<sup>−j2πft</sup> dt = ∫ x(t) e<sup>−j2π(f − f<sub>c</sub>)t</sup> dt = X(f − f<sub>c</sub>)
cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) = ½e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup> + ½e<sup>−j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>
so  x(t) cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) ↔ ½X(f − f<sub>c</sub>) + ½X(f + f<sub>c</sub>)

answer: Meaning: multiplying by a carrier moves the message spectrum to ±f<sub>c</sub> at half height. This one line is the whole of modulation in frequency, and multiplying again by cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) at the receiver brings a copy back to 0 Hz (coherent detection).

answer.text: Convolution theorem: if y(t) = x(t) * h(t) = ∫ x(τ)h(t − τ) dτ, then Y(f) = X(f)H(f). Proof in one line: transform the integral, substitute u = t − τ, and the double integral splits into X(f) times H(f). So a filter is a multiplication by H(f) in frequency; the dual statement, multiplication in time ↔ convolution in frequency, is the modulation theorem again.
answer.pre:
Y(f) = ∫∫ x(τ) h(t − τ) e<sup>−j2πft</sup> dτ dt
     = ∫ x(τ) e<sup>−j2πfτ</sup> dτ · ∫ h(u) e<sup>−j2πfu</sup> du = X(f) H(f)

answer: Parseval (Rayleigh energy theorem): ∫ |x(t)|² dt = ∫ |X(f)|² df, both in V²·s (energy per ohm). |X(f)|² is the energy spectral density, and the theorem lets the energy in any band be found from the spectrum.

head: Quantity
Time side
Frequency side
rows: two copies of ¼ each: 2×10<sup>−3</sup> V²·s

answer: Conclusion: linearity builds spectra piece by piece, the modulation theorem moves them, the convolution theorem filters them, and Parseval accounts for their energy. Check: the modulated pulse carries exactly half the energy (2×10<sup>−3</sup> of 4×10<sup>−3</sup> V²·s), as the ½ in the modulation theorem predicts.

bank.q: Define a random variable, its CDF and its PDF, and give the expressions for mean and variance.
outline: Random variable as a mapping from outcomes to real numbers
CDF F<sub>X</sub>(x) = P(X ≤ x): non-decreasing, limits 0 and 1, right-continuous
PDF f<sub>X</sub> = dF<sub>X</sub>/dx, total area 1, P(a < X ≤ b) as an integral
Mean μ = ∫x f<sub>X</sub>(x)dx and variance σ² = E[X²] − μ²
Worked instances: uniform and Gaussian
answer: Random variable: a rule X that assigns a real number X(s) to each outcome s of an experiment. Example: the noise voltage read at one instant, or the number of errors in a 1000-bit packet.

CDF: F<sub>X</sub>(x) = P(X ≤ x). Properties: 0 ≤ F<sub>X</sub>(x) ≤ 1; F<sub>X</sub>(−∞) = 0 and F<sub>X</sub>(∞) = 1; non-decreasing (x<sub>1</sub> < x<sub>2</sub> gives F(x<sub>1</sub>) ≤ F(x<sub>2</sub>)); right-continuous; and P(a < X ≤ b) = F<sub>X</sub>(b) − F<sub>X</sub>(a).

PDF (continuous X): f<sub>X</sub>(x) = dF<sub>X</sub>(x)/dx. Properties: f<sub>X</sub>(x) ≥ 0; ∫ f<sub>X</sub>(x) dx = 1 over all x; P(a < X ≤ b) = ∫ f<sub>X</sub>(x) dx from a to b. The PDF is a density: its height may exceed 1, and P(X = x) = 0 for any single x. A discrete X has a mass function p<sub>X</sub>(x) = P(X = x) instead.

bank.q: Define a wide-sense stationary process and state the Wiener–Khinchin theorem with the properties of the autocorrelation function.
outline: Ensemble, sample function; time and ensemble averages
WSS: constant mean, R depends only on τ
Properties: R(0) = mean power, R(−τ) = R(τ), |R(τ)| ≤ R(0), periodic component
Wiener–Khinchin: S<sub>X</sub>(f) and R<sub>X</sub>(τ) are a Fourier pair; power = area under S<sub>X</sub>
S<sub>X</sub> real, even, non-negative; example: random-phase sinusoid
WSS does not imply ergodic or Gaussian
answer: A random process X(t) is an ensemble of sample functions; fixing t gives a random variable. Its mean is μ<sub>X</sub>(t) = E[X(t)] and its autocorrelation R<sub>X</sub>(t<sub>1</sub>, t<sub>2</sub>) = E[X(t<sub>1</sub>)X(t<sub>2</sub>)], both ensemble averages.

Wide-sense stationary (WSS): (i) μ<sub>X</sub>(t) = μ<sub>X</sub>, a constant; (ii) R<sub>X</sub>(t + τ, t) = R<sub>X</sub>(τ), depending only on the gap τ. Strict-sense stationarity (all joint distributions shift-invariant) implies WSS; the reverse holds for Gaussian processes.

answer.text: Properties of R<sub>X</sub>(τ) for a real WSS process, with the reason for each:

head: Property
Why
rows: E[X(t − τ)X(t)] = E[X(t')X(t' + τ)] with t' = t − τ
the product repeats with the period

answer: Wiener–Khinchin theorem: for a WSS process the power spectral density is the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation, S<sub>X</sub>(f) = ∫ R<sub>X</sub>(τ) e<sup>−j2πfτ</sup> dτ, and R<sub>X</sub>(τ) = ∫ S<sub>X</sub>(f) e<sup>j2πfτ</sup> df. At τ = 0: P = R<sub>X</sub>(0) = ∫ S<sub>X</sub>(f) df, so the area under the PSD is the power.

Properties of S<sub>X</sub>(f): real and even (transform of a real, even function); never negative (the power through any narrow filter, S<sub>X</sub>(f)Δf, cannot be negative); through a filter, S<sub>Y</sub>(f) = |H(f)|² S<sub>X</sub>(f).

answer.pre:
E[X(t)] = 0 for every t
R<sub>X</sub>(τ) = (A²/2) cos(2πf<sub>0</sub>τ) = 2 cos(2π·1000τ) W     → WSS
R<sub>X</sub>(0) = 2 W,  R<sub>X</sub>(0.25 ms) = 0,  R<sub>X</sub>(0.5 ms) = −2 W
S<sub>X</sub>(f) = 1·δ(f − 1000) + 1·δ(f + 1000)  W

answer: Ergodicity is a further property: time averages of one sample function equal the ensemble averages. WSS does not guarantee it; a random DC level is WSS but each recording shows only its own level.
Check: the area under S<sub>X</sub> in the example is 1 + 1 = 2 W = R<sub>X</sub>(0), and |R<sub>X</sub>(0.5 ms)| = 2 W does not exceed R<sub>X</sub>(0).

bank.q: Define noise figure and noise temperature, relate them, and write the Friis formula for cascaded stages.
outline: F = SNR<sub>in</sub>/SNR<sub>out</sub> with a matched source at T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K; NF = 10 log<sub>10</sub> F
F = N<sub>o</sub>/(G kT<sub>0</sub>B); T<sub>e</sub> from the added noise kT<sub>e</sub>B referred to the input
T<sub>e</sub> = (F − 1)T<sub>0</sub> and F = 1 + T<sub>e</sub>/T<sub>0</sub>
Friis in F and in T<sub>e</sub>; first stage dominates
Lossy line: F = L at T<sub>0</sub>; numerical example
answer: Noise factor: F = SNR<sub>in</sub>/SNR<sub>out</sub>, a linear ratio measured with a matched source at T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K. Noise figure: NF = 10 log<sub>10</sub> F in dB. F ≥ 1 because the device amplifies signal and input noise alike and then adds its own noise.

answer.text: Noise powers: with input noise kT<sub>0</sub>B, gain G and added noise N<sub>a</sub> at the output,
answer.pre: F = (S<sub>i</sub>/kT<sub>0</sub>B) / (G S<sub>i</sub> / (G kT<sub>0</sub>B + N<sub>a</sub>)) = 1 + N<sub>a</sub>/(G kT<sub>0</sub>B)

answer.text: Noise temperature: write the added noise as if it came from a resistor at T<sub>e</sub> at the input, N<sub>a</sub> = G kT<sub>e</sub>B. Then
answer.pre:
F = 1 + T<sub>e</sub>/T<sub>0</sub>        T<sub>e</sub> = (F − 1) T<sub>0</sub>
F = 2 (NF = 3.01 dB)   →  T<sub>e</sub> = 290 K
NF = 1 dB (F = 1.259)  →  T<sub>e</sub> = 75.1 K

answer.text: Friis formula for a cascade (linear F and G):
answer.pre:
F = F<sub>1</sub> + (F<sub>2</sub> − 1)/G<sub>1</sub> + (F<sub>3</sub> − 1)/(G<sub>1</sub>G<sub>2</sub>) + …
T<sub>e</sub> = T<sub>e1</sub> + T<sub>e2</sub>/G<sub>1</sub> + T<sub>e3</sub>/(G<sub>1</sub>G<sub>2</sub>) + …

answer: Each stage's added noise is referred to the input by dividing by the gain in front of it, so a high-gain, low-noise first stage makes the later terms small.

answer.text: Example: stage 1 G = 20 dB, NF = 3 dB; stage 2 NF = 6 dB.

answer: A lossy line of loss L at T<sub>0</sub> has F = L and G = 1/L: a 3 dB cable has F = 1.995 and T<sub>e</sub> = 288.6 K, and placed before the first amplifier it multiplies every later term by L.
Check by the temperature form: 288.6 + 864.5/100 = 297.3 K, the same as (F − 1)T<sub>0</sub>.

bank.q: A band-pass signal is x(t) = A·m(t)·cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) with m(t) band-limited to W hertz and W much less than f<sub>c</sub>. Find its Hilbert transform, analytic signal and complex envelope, sketch the spectra, and evaluate them for A = 2 V, m(t) = cos(2π×10³t) and f<sub>c</sub> = 1 MHz.
outline: Hilbert transform of a low-pass m(t) times a carrier: x̂(t) = A·m(t)·sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) (W < f<sub>c</sub>)
Analytic signal x<sub>a</sub> = A·m(t)·e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>
Complex envelope x̃(t) = A·m(t), real, so x<sub>Q</sub> = 0
Spectra: ½A M(f ∓ f<sub>c</sub>); positive half doubled; shifted to 0 Hz
Numbers: tones at 0.999 and 1.001 MHz; x̃ = 2 cos(2π×10³t)
answer: Spectrum of x(t): by the modulation theorem X(f) = (A/2)M(f − f<sub>c</sub>) + (A/2)M(f + f<sub>c</sub>). Because W < f<sub>c</sub>, the copy at +f<sub>c</sub> lies entirely at positive frequencies and the copy at −f<sub>c</sub> entirely at negative ones.

answer.text: Hilbert transform: multiply each half by −j sgn f.
answer.pre:
X̂(f) = −j(A/2)M(f − f<sub>c</sub>) + j(A/2)M(f + f<sub>c</sub>)
     = transform of A·m(t)·sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t)      since sin = (e<sup>jθ</sup> − e<sup>−jθ</sup>)/2j
x̂(t) = A·m(t)·sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t)

answer: Analytic signal: x<sub>a</sub>(t) = x + j x̂ = A·m(t)[cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) + j sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t)] = A·m(t)e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>. Its spectrum is X<sub>a</sub>(f) = A·M(f − f<sub>c</sub>): only the positive copy, at twice the height of the copy in X(f).

Complex envelope: x̃(t) = x<sub>a</sub>(t)e<sup>−j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup> = A·m(t), with spectrum X̃(f) = A·M(f), centred on 0 Hz. It is real, so x<sub>I</sub>(t) = A·m(t) and x<sub>Q</sub>(t) = 0; the envelope is |A·m(t)|. The band-pass signal occupies f<sub>c</sub> − W to f<sub>c</sub> + W, width 2W; the complex envelope occupies −W to W.

answer: Why only the carrier is shifted (the condition W < f<sub>c</sub>): the Hilbert transformer multiplies by −j on every positive frequency. The copy (A/2)M(f − f<sub>c</sub>) lies wholly at positive f only if f<sub>c</sub> − W > 0. If W were larger than f<sub>c</sub>, part of that copy would spill below 0 Hz, would be multiplied by +j instead, and x̂(t) would no longer equal A·m(t)·sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t). That is why the narrowband condition is stated.

bank.q: White noise of two-sided PSD N₀/2 = 10⁻²⁰ W/Hz passes through an ideal band-pass filter of bandwidth B = 1 MHz centred at 100 MHz. Find the output noise power and the SNR if the signal power at the filter output is 1 pW. Also give the power of the in-phase and quadrature noise components.
outline: Output PSD N₀/2 in two bands of width B at ±100 MHz
Noise power = 2 × (N₀/2) × B = N₀B = 2×10⁻¹⁴ W
n<sub>I</sub> and n<sub>Q</sub>: PSD N₀ over |f| < B/2, power N₀B each
Units W/Hz × Hz = W; the centre frequency does not matter
answer: Output PSD: S<sub>Y</sub>(f) = |H(f)|² S<sub>X</sub>(f) = 10<sup>−20</sup> W/Hz for 99.5 MHz < |f| < 100.5 MHz, and 0 elsewhere: two bands, each 1 MHz wide, one at +100 MHz and one at −100 MHz.

answer.text: Noise power = area under S<sub>Y</sub>:
answer.pre:
N = 2 × (N₀/2) × B = 2 × 10<sup>−20</sup> × 10<sup>6</sup> = 2×10<sup>−14</sup> W
same as N₀B with N₀ = 2×10<sup>−20</sup> W/Hz

answer.text: SNR, as a ratio and in dB:

answer: Only the width B matters, not the 100 MHz centre: the same filter at 10 MHz would pass the same 2×10<sup>−14</sup> W. For comparison, a resistor at 290 K has N₀ = kT = 4.0×10<sup>−21</sup> W/Hz; this noise is 5 times stronger, equal to thermal noise at N₀/k = 2×10<sup>−20</sup>/1.38×10<sup>−23</sup> = 1449 K.

In-phase and quadrature components: the filtered noise is narrowband, n(t) = n<sub>I</sub>(t)cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) − n<sub>Q</sub>(t)sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) with f<sub>c</sub> = 100 MHz. Each of n<sub>I</sub>, n<sub>Q</sub> has PSD S<sub>N</sub>(f − f<sub>c</sub>) + S<sub>N</sub>(f + f<sub>c</sub>) = N₀ = 2×10<sup>−20</sup> W/Hz for |f| < B/2 = 0.5 MHz.
Power of each: 2×10<sup>−20</sup> × (2 × 0.5×10<sup>6</sup>) = 2×10<sup>−14</sup> W, the same as n(t). They are zero-mean Gaussian, and their envelope √(n<sub>I</sub>² + n<sub>Q</sub>²) is Rayleigh.

answer.text: Autocorrelation of the filtered noise, the inverse transform of two rectangles of height N₀/2 and width B at ±f<sub>c</sub>:
answer.pre:
R<sub>N</sub>(τ) = N₀B sinc(Bτ) cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>τ) = 2×10<sup>−14</sup> sinc(10<sup>6</sup>τ) cos(2π·10<sup>8</sup>τ)  W
R<sub>N</sub>(0) = 2×10<sup>−14</sup> W = the noise power;  envelope sinc(10<sup>6</sup>τ) first zero at τ = 1/B = 1 µs

answer: So samples of the band-pass noise more than about 1 µs apart are nearly uncorrelated, while within that time the noise looks like a 100 MHz sinusoid with slowly wandering amplitude and phase: exactly the n<sub>I</sub>, n<sub>Q</sub> picture.

answer.text: Sensitivity: the smallest signal that gives SNR = 10 dB (a factor 10) at the filter output:
answer.pre:
S<sub>min</sub> = 10 × N = 10 × 2×10<sup>−14</sup> = 2×10<sup>−13</sup> W = −97.0 dBm
the given 1 pW (−90.0 dBm) is 7.0 dB above this, so the SNR is 10 + 7.0 = 17.0 dB

answer: Check the units: (W/Hz) × Hz = W. And 10 log<sub>10</sub>(2×10<sup>−14</sup>/10<sup>−3</sup>) = −107.0 dBm, so −90.0 − (−107.0) = 17.0 dB, matching 10 log<sub>10</sub> 50.

outline: Gains from dB to ratios: G₁ = 100, G₂ = 10
NF = 3.21 dB; T<sub>e</sub> = 1.093 × 290 = 317.0 K; check with the temperature form
Without the RF amplifier: F = 10 + 3/10 = 10.3, NF = 10.13 dB
Later stages contribute little because of the gain in front
answer: Convert gains to linear: G₁ = 10<sup>20/10</sup> = 100, G₂ = 10<sup>10/10</sup> = 10. The noise factors are already linear: F₁ = 2, F₂ = 10, F₃ = 4. The IF amplifier's gain is not needed: nothing follows it.

answer.text: Friis formula, term by term:

answer: Noise figure: NF = 10 log<sub>10</sub> 2.093 = 3.21 dB. Stage 1 alone has 10 log<sub>10</sub> 2 = 3.01 dB, so the mixer and IF stage together add only 0.20 dB.

answer.text: Noise temperature, and the check with the temperature form of Friis (T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K):
Without the RF amplifier the mixer is first:

answer: Interpretation: the 20 dB RF amplifier divides the mixer's large excess noise (F₂ − 1 = 9) by 100, so the receiver noise figure drops from 10.13 dB to 3.21 dB, an improvement of 6.92 dB. This is why a receiver puts a low-noise amplifier ahead of the mixer.

answer.text: Noise referred to the input, for an IF bandwidth B = 200 kHz and a source at 290 K:

answer: The dB route works because F = (total input-referred noise)/(source noise) = (T<sub>0</sub> + T<sub>e</sub>)/T<sub>0</sub> = 607.0/290 = 2.093. With the RF amplifier removed the same 20 dB SNR would need 10.13 − 3.21 = 6.92 dB more signal, about 4.9 times the power.

bank.q: A stationary process has autocorrelation R<sub>X</sub>(τ) = P·e<sup>−a|τ|</sup> with a > 0. Find its power spectral density, its total power, and the power in the band |f| ≤ a/2π. Evaluate for P = 1 mW and a = 1000 s⁻¹.
outline: Wiener–Khinchin on the two-sided exponential
S<sub>X</sub>(f) = 2aP/(a² + 4π²f²)
Total power ∫S<sub>X</sub> df = P = R<sub>X</sub>(0)
Band power (2P/π)tan<sup>−1</sup>(2πf<sub>1</sub>/a) = P/2 at f<sub>1</sub> = a/2π
Numbers: S(0) = 2 µW/Hz, f<sub>1</sub> = 159.2 Hz, 0.5 mW

answer.text: Wiener–Khinchin: S<sub>X</sub>(f) = ∫ P e<sup>−a|τ|</sup> e<sup>−j2πfτ</sup> dτ. Split at τ = 0:
answer.pre:
∫<sub>0</sub><sup>∞</sup> P e<sup>−(a + j2πf)τ</sup> dτ = P/(a + j2πf)
∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>0</sup> P e<sup>(a − j2πf)τ</sup> dτ = P/(a − j2πf)
S<sub>X</sub>(f) = P[1/(a + j2πf) + 1/(a − j2πf)] = 2aP/(a² + 4π²f²)

answer: S<sub>X</sub>(f) is real, even and positive, as a PSD must be. It is not flat: it falls to half its peak at 2πf = a, that is at f = a/2π, and as 1/f² beyond.

answer.text: Total power, using ∫ dx/(1 + x²) = π over all x with x = 2πf/a:
answer.pre:
∫ S<sub>X</sub>(f) df = (2P/a) ∫ df/(1 + (2πf/a)²) = (2P/a)(a/2π)(π) = P
which equals R<sub>X</sub>(0) = P e<sup>0</sup> = P

answer.text: Power in |f| ≤ f<sub>1</sub>:
answer.pre:
P<sub>band</sub> = (2P/a)(a/2π) [tan<sup>−1</sup>(2πf/a)] from −f<sub>1</sub> to f<sub>1</sub> = (2P/π) tan<sup>−1</sup>(2πf<sub>1</sub>/a)
at f<sub>1</sub> = a/2π:  P<sub>band</sub> = (2P/π)(π/4) = P/2

answer.text: Numbers, P = 1 mW and a = 1000 s<sup>−1</sup>:

answer: Interpretation: a correlation time of 1/a = 1 ms gives a spectrum about 159 Hz wide; a faster-decaying R<sub>X</sub>(τ) (larger a) spreads the power over more frequencies, the time–bandwidth trade of the Fourier transform.

answer.text: Through a filter: pass X(t) through an RC low-pass with f<sub>0</sub> = a/2π = 159.2 Hz, |H|² = 1/(1 + u²) with u = 2πf/a:
answer.pre:
S<sub>Y</sub>(f) = |H(f)|² S<sub>X</sub>(f) = (2P/a) / (1 + u²)²
P<sub>Y</sub> = (2P/a)(a/2π) ∫ du/(1 + u²)² = (P/π)(π/2) = P/2 = 0.5 mW

answer: The RC filter passes 0.5 mW, the same as the ideal filter of width a/2π above, although its shape is different: the RC filter keeps some power beyond 159.2 Hz but loses some below it.

Correlation time: R<sub>X</sub>(τ) falls to 1/e of P, 0.368 mW, at τ = 1/a = 1 ms, and to 0.1 mW at τ = (ln 10)/a = 2.30 ms. Samples 5 ms apart have R = e<sup>−5</sup> × 1 mW = 6.7 µW, so they are nearly uncorrelated.
Check: S<sub>X</sub>(159.2 Hz) = 2aP/(a² + a²) = P/a = 1×10<sup>−6</sup> W/Hz, exactly half of S<sub>X</sub>(0) = 2×10<sup>−6</sup> W/Hz.

bank.q: Explain why an ideal white noise source cannot exist in practice, and show how the concept is still used with a finite bandwidth and the equivalent noise bandwidth.
outline: Flat PSD for all f gives infinite power and R(τ) = (N₀/2)δ(τ)
Thermal noise is flat only up to about a terahertz at room temperature (quantum correction)
Band-limiting: power N₀B, any centre frequency
Equivalent noise bandwidth B<sub>n</sub> = ∫|H|²df/|H|<sub>max</sub>²; RC result (π/2)f<sub>3dB</sub>
Numbers: RC with 10 kHz cut-off; bandwidth-for-SNR consequence
answer: Definition: white noise has S(f) = N₀/2 at every frequency, so R(τ) = (N₀/2)δ(τ). Its power would be ∫ S(f) df over all f = ∞, and an infinite-power source cannot exist. White noise is therefore a model, not a signal.

answer.text: Why the model is still good: thermal noise is flat to a very high frequency. Its exact density carries the factor x/(e<sup>x</sup> − 1) with x = hf/kT. At T = 290 K:

answer: Every radio receiver works far below a terahertz, so over its band the noise is flat to better than 1 %: white over the band that matters.
Band-limiting: a filter of bandwidth B passes power N₀B (two-sided: (N₀/2) × 2B). For thermal noise N₀ = kT, giving the familiar kTB. Only the width matters; the centre frequency does not.

answer.text: Real filters are not rectangular. The equivalent noise bandwidth B<sub>n</sub> is the width of an ideal filter, with the same peak power gain, that passes the same white-noise power:
answer.pre:
B<sub>n</sub> = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>∞</sup> |H(f)|² df / |H|<sub>max</sub>²
RC low-pass, |H|² = 1/(1 + (f/f<sub>0</sub>)²):  B<sub>n</sub> = f<sub>0</sub> ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>∞</sup> dx/(1 + x²) = (π/2) f<sub>0</sub> = 1/(4RC)

answer.text: Numbers: N₀ = 4.0×10<sup>−21</sup> W/Hz (a 290 K source) and an RC filter with f<sub>3dB</sub> = 10 kHz:

answer: Using the 3-dB bandwidth for the RC filter would understate its noise by a factor π/2, 1.96 dB, because the gentle skirts keep passing noise above f<sub>3dB</sub>.

Consequence for design: noise power grows in proportion to bandwidth, so a receiver should be no wider than its signal; doubling B costs 3 dB of SNR. Wideband FM is the exception that trades extra bandwidth for SNR after demodulation.

answer.text: What band-limiting does in time: white noise through an ideal low-pass filter of bandwidth B has
answer.pre:
S(f) = N₀/2 for |f| ≤ B   →   R(τ) = N₀B sinc(2Bτ)
R(0) = N₀B (finite power);  zeros at τ = 1/(2B), 2/(2B), …
as B → ∞, N₀B sinc(2Bτ) → (N₀/2)δ(τ), the white-noise autocorrelation

answer: So band-limited white noise is the physical object: its samples taken 1/(2B) apart are uncorrelated (and, being Gaussian, independent). For B = 10 kHz that spacing is 50 µs.
Quick rule in dBm: thermal noise power = −174 dBm/Hz + 10 log<sub>10</sub>B at 290 K. For B = 10 kHz: −174.0 + 40.0 = −134.0 dBm, which is 4.0×10<sup>−17</sup> W, the ideal-filter row of the table.

bank.q: Explain the complex-envelope or low-pass equivalent approach for band-pass signals and systems, and show why it simplifies the analysis of modulation, filtering and noise.
outline: Analytic signal, then shift by f<sub>c</sub> to get x̃(t)
Canonical form x = x<sub>I</sub>cos − x<sub>Q</sub>sin; envelope and phase
Band-pass filter → low-pass filter on x̃, with ỹ = ½x̃ * h̃
Modulation and demodulation become multiplication by e<sup>±j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>
Noise: n<sub>I</sub>, n<sub>Q</sub> Gaussian with the same power
Sample-rate saving with numbers; narrowband condition B ≪ f<sub>c</sub>
answer: Start: a real band-pass signal x(t) with spectrum in a band B around ±f<sub>c</sub>, B ≪ f<sub>c</sub>. Form the analytic signal x<sub>a</sub> = x + j x̂ (positive frequencies only, doubled), then remove the carrier: x̃(t) = x<sub>a</sub>(t)e<sup>−j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup> = x<sub>I</sub>(t) + j x<sub>Q</sub>(t). Its spectrum lies in −B/2 to B/2.

Representation: x(t) = Re{x̃(t)e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>} = x<sub>I</sub> cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) − x<sub>Q</sub> sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) = a(t) cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + φ(t)), with envelope a = |x̃| and phase φ = ∠x̃. The carrier is known, so x̃ carries all the information.

answer.text: Modulation in this language: each scheme is just a choice of x̃(t).

answer: Filtering: a band-pass filter h(t) = Re{h̃(t)e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>} acts on the envelope as ỹ = ½ x̃ * h̃, a low-pass convolution; the real output is y = Re{ỹ e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>}. No carrier terms appear in the working.

Up- and downconversion: the transmitter forms x<sub>I</sub>cos − x<sub>Q</sub>sin; the receiver multiplies by 2cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) and −2sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) and low-pass filters to recover x<sub>I</sub> and x<sub>Q</sub>. Example: a 2 V tone at 1.001 MHz, seen about f<sub>c</sub> = 1 MHz, gives x̃ = 2e<sup>j2π(1000)t</sup>: at t = 0.125 ms, I = Q = 1.414 V.

Noise: narrowband Gaussian noise of PSD N₀/2 in the band becomes n<sub>I</sub> + j n<sub>Q</sub>, each Gaussian, low-pass to B/2, PSD N₀, power N₀B, the same as n(t). So SNR calculations for AM, FM and digital receivers can be done entirely at baseband.

answer.text: Sample-rate saving, for one FM channel of B = 200 kHz at f<sub>c</sub> = 100 MHz:
answer.pre:
band-pass signal sampled directly: more than 2(f<sub>c</sub> + B/2) = 2 × 100.1 MHz = 200.2 Msamples/s
I and Q, each low-pass to 100 kHz: 2 × 200 ksamples/s = 400 ksamples/s
ratio 200.2×10<sup>6</sup> / 4×10<sup>5</sup> ≈ 500

answer.text: Worked check of the ½ on an ideal band-pass filter of width B at f<sub>c</sub> (gain 1 in the band):
answer.pre:
h(t) = 2B sinc(Bt) cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t)          (two unit rectangles of width B at ±f<sub>c</sub>)
h̃(t) = 2B sinc(Bt),   H̃(f) = 2 for |f| < B/2
Ỹ(f) = ½ X̃(f) H̃(f) = X̃(f) inside the band     → unity gain, as it must be

answer: Without the ½ the same filter would appear to double the envelope, a 6 dB error; this check is the quickest way to confirm which convention a textbook uses.
Limits: the method needs B ≪ f<sub>c</sub> so the two spectral halves do not overlap, a fixed reference f<sub>c</sub> (the envelope changes with the choice), and one consistent convention for the ½.
Check on the canonical form: for x = 2cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°), x̃ = 1.732 + j1, and 1.732cos − 1·sin = 2cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t + 30°).

bank.q: Derive the canonical representation of a real band-pass signal in terms of its in-phase and quadrature components, and state the properties of their spectra.
outline: Analytic signal and complex envelope; x = Re{x̃e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>}
Expand to x<sub>I</sub>cos − x<sub>Q</sub>sin; x<sub>I</sub> = x cos + x̂ sin, x<sub>Q</sub> = x̂ cos − x sin
Recover by multiplying by 2cos and −2sin and low-pass filtering
Spectra: low-pass, width B/2; X<sub>I</sub>(f) = X(f − f<sub>c</sub>) + X(f + f<sub>c</sub>) when the spectrum is symmetric about f<sub>c</sub>; powers
Numerical check
answer: Step 1, analytic signal: x<sub>a</sub>(t) = x(t) + j x̂(t), whose spectrum is 2X(f) for f > 0 and 0 for f < 0. It contains the carrier.

Step 2, complex envelope: x̃(t) = x<sub>a</sub>(t)e<sup>−j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>, spectrum X̃(f) = 2X(f + f<sub>c</sub>) for f + f<sub>c</sub> > 0, a low-pass spectrum in −B/2 to B/2. Write x̃ = x<sub>I</sub> + j x<sub>Q</sub>.

answer.text: Step 3, back to x(t): since x = Re{x<sub>a</sub>} = Re{x̃ e<sup>j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>},
answer.pre:
x(t) = Re{(x<sub>I</sub> + j x<sub>Q</sub>)(cos 2πf<sub>c</sub>t + j sin 2πf<sub>c</sub>t)}
     = x<sub>I</sub>(t) cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) − x<sub>Q</sub>(t) sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t)

answer.text: Step 4, I and Q in terms of x and x̂ (take real and imaginary parts of x<sub>a</sub>e<sup>−j2πf<sub>c</sub>t</sup>):

bank.q: Distinguish between uncorrelated and statistically independent random variables, and justify the Gaussian model for receiver noise using the central limit theorem.
outline: Uncorrelated: E[XY] = E[X]E[Y]; independent: joint PDF factorises
Independence implies uncorrelated, not the reverse; counterexample Y = X²
Jointly Gaussian: uncorrelated implies independent
CLT statement and conditions; numerical check with a sum of uniforms
Thermal noise as a sum of many electron contributions; Gaussian preserved by linear filters
Limits: impulsive and burst noise, interference
answer: Uncorrelated: cov(X, Y) = E[XY] − E[X]E[Y] = 0. Independent: f<sub>XY</sub>(x, y) = f<sub>X</sub>(x)f<sub>Y</sub>(y) for all x, y, so every function of X is independent of every function of Y.

Independence implies uncorrelated: E[XY] = ∫∫ xy f<sub>X</sub>f<sub>Y</sub> dx dy = E[X]E[Y]. The reverse fails. Counterexample: X uniform on [−1, 1] and Y = X². E[X] = 0 and E[XY] = E[X³] = 0, so cov = 0, yet Y is completely fixed by X: P(Y > 0.25 | X = 0.9) = 1 while P(Y > 0.25) = P(|X| > 0.5) = 0.5.

Special case: if X and Y are jointly Gaussian and uncorrelated, the joint PDF factorises into the two marginals, so they are independent. Two variables that are each Gaussian but not jointly Gaussian need not be.

Central limit theorem: the sum of n independent, identically distributed variables with finite variance, standardised, tends to N(0, 1) as n grows; for unequal terms a condition such as Lindeberg's keeps any single term from dominating.

answer.text: Numerical check: S = sum of 12 independent uniforms on [−0.5, 0.5] has mean 0 and variance 12 × 1/12 = 1. Its exact tails (Irwin–Hall distribution) against the Gaussian:

answer: Twelve terms already match near the centre; the far tails converge more slowly. A noise voltage is the sum of the tiny contributions of an enormous number of electrons, so its distribution is Gaussian to high accuracy. A linear filter forms weighted sums of Gaussian samples, so filtered Gaussian noise stays Gaussian, and only its mean and autocorrelation (or PSD) are needed.

Limits of the model: impulsive noise (ignition, lightning) and burst noise are dominated by a few large events, so the CLT does not apply and their tails are far heavier; strong interference from one transmitter is a single term, not a sum. Error-rate formulas built on AWGN are then optimistic.
